Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Blind women are being trained to use their sensitive touch to help detect breast cancer earlier and more precisely than doctors. The blind assistants use tape strips with braille coordinates to accurately locate cancerous lumps . The program, called "Discovering Hands," is the brainchild of German gynecologist Dr. Frank Hoffmann. Two years ago, he created Braille strips as a system of orientation, allowing the blind to carry out breast examinations. Using these strips blind women are trained to become Medical Tactile Examiners (MTUs) because they are more able to detect smaller lumps than sighted doctors. Hoffman argues that because of their disability, the blind can possess a more acutely developed sense of touch, which has proved to be a valuable asset in breast examinations. Once the strips are placed along specific areas of the breast, they are then used to report a precise location to the doctor as the MTU reads their Braille coordinates. "We are turning a disability into a gift,"  Dr. Hoffmann told CNN. "It's like the game Battleship," he added. "You have the exact location." A study at the Essen University's women's clinic, Germany, concluded that MTUs found more and smaller tumors than doctors in 450 cases. The identification of smaller lumps allows earlier diagnosis and more effective treatment. Another advantage of having MTUs is that they are able to dedicate more time to examining a patient. Dr. Hoffman said he had previously been able to spend only a few minutes on each examination due to his other commitments, whereas MTUs can commit half an hour. Training takes place at the BFW occupational school in Düren, west Germany, a center for those who are no longer able to continue their profession because of visual impairment or blindness. So far, ten blind women have qualified as MTUs. One of the women, Marie-Luise Voll, 57, told CNN: " The work brings me a lot of joy." Voll had previously practiced as a nurse before losing her sight in 2007, but used the experience when training at Düren for her new role. The highly personal nature of the procedure means that only women will be trained. The MTUs report to the doctor - for whom they act as an assistant not a replacement - who then uses this information as part of their ultimate diagnosis. If an abnormality is located the doctor will decide how to proceed, with ultrasounds and mammography being the most frequent course of action. The testing phase of the project between 2006 and 2008 has now been completed in Germany. The hope is that twenty trained MTUs will qualify every year after 2010. The program has been acclaimed as a success by both patients and practitioners in Germany. Health services in Europe including Ireland, France, Denmark and Austria have also registered interest in starting an equivalent of their own, Hoffman said.

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Blind women are learning to use their heightened tactile sensitivity to identify breast cancer sooner and pinpoint suspicious growths more accurately than physicians.

The initiative, known as **“Discovering Hands,”** was developed by German gynecologist Dr. Frank Hoffmann. Two years earlier, Hoffmann designed adhesive strips marked with Braille coordinates to provide an orientation grid during breast examinations. By reading these coordinates, blind examiners can tell doctors the exact position of a lump.

Women who complete the training become **Medical Tactile Examiners (MTUs)**. According to Hoffmann, blindness can lead to a particularly refined sense of touch, enabling MTUs to notice smaller lumps than sighted doctors can detect. The Braille strips are applied to designated sections of the breast, allowing the examiner to describe the precise location of any abnormality.

“We are turning a disability into a gift,” Hoffmann told CNN. He compared the method to the board game Battleship because it provides an exact set of coordinates.

Research involving 450 cases at the women’s clinic of Essen University in Germany found that MTUs detected a greater number of tumors—and smaller ones—than doctors did. Finding smaller lumps can result in an earlier diagnosis and improve the effectiveness of treatment.

MTUs also have more time available for each patient. Hoffmann said that his other responsibilities had previously limited him to only a few minutes per breast examination, while a tactile examiner can spend about 30 minutes on the procedure.

Training is provided at the BFW vocational school in Düren, western Germany. The center supports people who can no longer remain in their former occupations because they have become visually impaired or blind. To date, 10 blind women have qualified as MTUs.

One graduate, 57-year-old Marie-Luise Voll, told CNN that the job gives her great joy. Voll had worked as a nurse before losing her vision in 2007, and she drew on that professional background while preparing for her new position in Düren.

Because breast examinations are highly intimate, the program trains only women. MTUs serve as assistants to doctors rather than replacing them. They communicate their findings to the physician, who incorporates the information into the final diagnosis. When an unusual area is discovered, the doctor determines the next step, most commonly an ultrasound or mammogram.

The project’s German trial period, which ran from 2006 through 2008, has ended. Organizers hope that, beginning after 2010, 20 MTUs will complete the program each year.

Patients and medical professionals in Germany have both praised the initiative as successful. Hoffmann said health services elsewhere in Europe—including Ireland, France, Denmark and Austria—have also expressed interest in creating similar programs.

# A new way to feel for breast cancer: Germany’s blind examiners bring a refined sense of touch

**DUISBURG, Germany —** Inside a quiet examination room, thin adhesive strips marked with raised coordinates are placed across a patient’s breast. Guided by those tactile markers, a specially trained examiner methodically moves her fingertips over the tissue, searching for anything unusual.

The examiner is blind — and in Germany’s “Discovering Hands” program, that is considered a professional advantage.

The initiative trains blind and visually impaired women to become Medical Tactile Examiners, or MTEs, using their highly developed sense of touch to help detect possible signs of breast cancer. The raised, Braille-style coordinate strips allow examiners to navigate the breast systematically and record the precise location of a lump or other abnormality for a physician.

The program was developed by German gynecologist Dr. Frank Hoffmann, who believed that the tactile sensitivity many blind women cultivate in daily life could be applied to clinical breast examinations. Trainees receive months of instruction in anatomy, communication and standardized examination techniques before working alongside doctors.

Each examination can take considerably longer than a routine physician’s breast check, allowing the examiner to assess tissue carefully and thoroughly. If she identifies a suspicious area, a doctor evaluates the finding and may recommend imaging or a biopsy.

Discovering Hands says its examiners can sometimes identify smaller tissue changes than those found during conventional clinical examinations. Medical experts stress, however, that the technique is an additional screening tool — not a replacement for mammography, ultrasound or other diagnostic tests.

For patients, the longer appointment can also offer something often scarce in busy medical settings: time. Examiners explain each stage of the process and encourage women to become more familiar with their own bodies.

The project has a second goal beyond early detection. Blind and visually impaired women often face limited employment opportunities, even when they are highly qualified. By turning tactile perception into a specialized medical skill, Discovering Hands offers participants a recognized role in health care.

The concept has since drawn interest beyond Germany, with versions of the training introduced or explored in other countries.

For the women doing the work, the examination is both painstaking and precise. Their fingertips move section by section, while the raised coordinate strips create a map that can be shared with a doctor.

In a field increasingly shaped by sophisticated imaging and artificial intelligence, Discovering Hands relies on a distinctly human diagnostic tool: touch.

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how visually impaired women are being trained as Medical Tactile Examiners to identify smaller breast tumors earlier than doctors, including details about the program’s origins, training, and results.
counterfactuals.output:
### Program origins

The approach was developed in Germany in the mid-2000s by gynecologist **Dr. Frank Hoffmann**, who was concerned that routine clinical breast examinations were often brief and inconsistent. He reasoned that blind and visually impaired women—who commonly develop highly refined touch and concentration skills—could be trained to perform a longer, standardized examination.

He founded the social enterprise **Discovering Hands**, which began qualifying visually impaired women as **Medical Tactile Examiners (MTEs)**. The model has since been introduced in several countries, including India, Austria, Colombia and Mexico.

### How MTEs are trained

In Germany, qualification generally lasts about **nine months**, combining classroom instruction with supervised clinical practice. Training covers:

- Breast anatomy and physiology  
- Benign and malignant breast changes  
- Systematic palpation at different tissue depths  
- Medical terminology and documentation  
- Patient communication, privacy and emotional support  
- Recognizing abnormalities and accurately describing their position, size, shape and texture  

MTEs use specially designed adhesive orientation strips placed on the breast. The raised markings create a coordinate grid, allowing the examiner to search the entire breast methodically and tell the physician exactly where an abnormality was felt.

An examination typically takes **30–45 minutes**, considerably longer than the few minutes often available during a routine physician visit. The MTE does not diagnose cancer. She documents her findings, after which a doctor reassesses suspicious areas and, when necessary, orders ultrasound, mammography or biopsy.

### Reported results

Early German clinical research involving roughly **450 patients** found that trained MTEs detected more palpable abnormalities than physicians performing conventional clinical breast examinations. Frequently reported findings from that study include:

- Sensitivity of about **96% for MTE examinations**, compared with roughly **74% for physicians’ examinations**
- Detection of approximately **28% more tissue abnormalities**
- Ability to find palpable changes around **6–8 millimeters**, while ordinary clinical examination often detects lumps closer to **10–20 millimeters**

These figures should be interpreted carefully: they concern detection of **palpable breast lesions**, not proof that every lesion was malignant, and results can vary by setting and study design. Evidence that the program reduces breast-cancer mortality is still limited.

The principal advantage is therefore not that MTEs replace doctors or mammography, but that a lengthy, standardized tactile examination may identify **smaller suspicious changes**, potentially allowing diagnostic imaging and treatment to begin sooner. The program also creates skilled, socially valued employment for women who often face substantial barriers in the conventional job market.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the “Discovering Hands” program: describe how Braille-marked tape helps blind female examiners locate breast lumps, why they may outperform sighted physicians, and how they work alongside doctors rather than replacing them.
counterfactuals.output:
## Discovering Hands

“Discovering Hands” is a German-founded program that trains blind and visually impaired women as **medical tactile examiners (MTEs)** for breast examinations.

### How the Braille-marked tape works

Before palpation, the examiner places standardized adhesive orientation strips on the patient’s chest and breasts. The strips carry raised or Braille-like markings that create a tactile coordinate system. Using these reference lines, the examiner can:

- Divide the breast into defined areas and examine each systematically.
- Identify the exact position of any unusual thickening or lump.
- Record its location, depth, size, and texture so a physician can recheck the same spot.

The tape therefore acts as a tactile map, helping ensure that no area is skipped and allowing findings to be communicated precisely.

### Why blind examiners may outperform sighted physicians

The program is based on the idea that people who rely heavily on touch often develop exceptional tactile discrimination. MTEs also receive specialized training and typically spend substantially longer on palpation than physicians can during a routine appointment. Studies and program evaluations have reported that trained MTEs may detect smaller tissue changes than are commonly found in a brief standard clinical breast examination.

Their advantage is not simply blindness itself; it comes from **intensive training, practiced touch, a structured method, and sufficient examination time**. The evidence is promising, but MTE examinations do not replace imaging or definitive diagnostic testing.

### Working alongside doctors

MTEs function as part of a medical team, usually in a gynecology or breast-care practice. They may take a focused history, perform and document the tactile examination, and report suspicious findings. A physician remains responsible for:

- Reviewing and confirming the findings.
- Deciding whether ultrasound, mammography, biopsy, or other testing is needed.
- Making the diagnosis and discussing treatment.

Thus, Discovering Hands presents tactile examiners as **specialized clinical assistants**, not replacements for doctors. The model both adds a potentially sensitive layer of breast assessment and creates skilled employment for visually impaired women.
